title: Range minimum queries: scanning each range vs a sparse table
problem_statement: Given n numbers a[0..n-1] and q queries (l, r) with 0 <= l <= r < n, return, for every query, min(a[l], a[l+1], ..., a[r]). This entry fixes q = n (offline: all queries are given with the input, but the algorithms answer them one at a time).

input.parameter: n = number of values (= number of queries q).
input.size_measure: n numbers plus q = n index pairs: Theta(n) words. Comparisons and index arithmetic are unit cost.

algorithms.name: scan each range
algorithms.idea: No preprocessing; answer each query by scanning a[l..r].
algorithms.pseudocode: for (l, r) in queries: m = a[l]; for i in l+1..r: m = min(m, a[i]); output m
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(q + sum of the query lengths); Theta(n^2) for q = n queries of length Theta(n), as in the scaling family (every range longer than n/2; total scanned length 0.75 n^2 within 0.5% at n = 800, 1200, 1600)

algorithms.name: sparse table
algorithms.idea: Precompute the minimum of every range whose length is a power of two (each level from the previous one). Any range [l, r] is the union of two such ranges of length 2^k, k = floor(log2(r - l + 1)), possibly overlapping, so a query takes two table lookups.
algorithms.pseudocode: T[0] = a; T[j][i] = min(T[j-1][i], T[j-1][i + 2^(j-1)]); query(l, r): k = floor(log2(r-l+1)); return min(T[k][l], T[k][r - 2^k + 1])
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n log n) preprocessing plus O(1) per query: Theta(n log n + q) = Theta(n log n) for q = n, on every input
algorithms.correctness: Induction on j: T[j][i] is the minimum of a[i .. i + 2^j - 1] because that range splits into two halves of length 2^(j-1). For a query, 2^k <= r - l + 1 < 2^(k+1), so the blocks [l, l + 2^k - 1] and [r - 2^k + 1, r] lie inside [l, r] and together cover it; min is idempotent, so the overlap does no harm. Presented as the <O(n log n), O(1)> sparse-table algorithm in Bender & Farach-Colton 2000.

relationship: Theta(n^2) -> Theta(n log n) for n values and n long queries. Preprocessing all power-of-two ranges turns each query into O(1) work. Linear preprocessing with O(1) queries is also possible: Bender & Farach-Colton 2000 reduce RMQ to LCA and back to RMQ with +-1 differences, and Fischer & Heun 2011 give a space-efficient scheme.

sources.title: Space-efficient preprocessing schemes for range minimum queries on static arrays

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with an independent oracle (an iterative segment tree in harness.py) on random values from [-1000, 1000] or [0, 4] (ties) with q = n queries mixing random ranges, single positions, short ranges and prefix/suffix/whole-array ranges, n = 0..8, 16, 50, 200, 2000 and 10000 (sparse table only above 2000). V2 by exact comparison counts (measure 'reported', round 2026-10-06c) on the long-query family (q = n ranges, each longer than n/2; the same seeded draws as the earlier timing fit). generate_scaling wraps every value in an instrumented type that counts each comparison the unchanged implementations make between values: `x < m` in the scan; in the sparse table the comparison inside each two-argument min() of the table build (CPython's min() calls __lt__ once per extra argument) plus `a <= b` per query. Index arithmetic is not counted. The counts equal closed forms computed from the instance alone: the sum of (r - l) over the queries for the scan (0.739-0.756 n^2 on the measured n), and sum_{j=1..K} (n - 2^j + 1) + n with K = floor(log2 n) for the sparse table, which is n log2 n - n + log2 n + 2 when n is a power of two (experiments/2026-10-06c_rmq_counts.py). Fits at tolerance 0.03: scan alpha = 1.001 against n^2 (n = 200..3200), rivals n log n (1.741), n^2 log n (0.931) and n^3 (0.668) rejected; sparse table alpha = 1.007 against n log n (n = 2000..128000), rivals n (1.113), n log^2 n (0.920) and n^2 (0.556) rejected. The log factor is therefore resolved. The earlier timing fit could not separate n log n from n (experiments/2026-10-07_rmq_probe.py: alpha = 0.989 against n log n and 1.100 against n).

caveats: The quadratic cost of scanning is a worst case. With short queries (length O(1)) scanning costs Theta(n) and beats the sparse table's Theta(n log n) preprocessing, so the pair is stated for q = n queries of length Theta(n). The sparse table's Theta(n log n) is dominated by preprocessing; with q >> n log n queries, both its per-query cost (O(1)) and the scan's (Theta(length)) matter. The algorithms here answer queries one at a time; offline algorithms that sort the queries are another option and are not considered.
notes: RMQ and lowest common ancestors in trees are linearly equivalent (Bender & Farach-Colton 2000). The sparse table also answers any idempotent associative range query (max, gcd, bitwise and/or) in O(1), but not sums, whose two blocks would double-count the overlap.
